The Zamzam Well is a well within the Grand Mosque complex in Mecca, about 20 metres east of the Kaaba according to published references, and it is the source of Zamzam water, which pilgrims drink and carry home. The well is described in published technical summaries as about 30 metres deep and 1.08 to 2.66 metres in diameter, tapping groundwater from the Wadi Ibrahim alluvium and from bedrock below. title: Location Within the Grand Mosque
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. The Zamzam Well stands inside the precinct of the Grand Mosque in Mecca, about 20 metres east of the Kaaba, and its opening was moved to a basement about 2.5 metres deep so that space above ground could be freed for pilgrims, according to published references. Zamzam water is distributed at points throughout the holy mosques, in cooled and uncooled dispensing containers and fountains for visitors, so that a pilgrim need not go to the well itself to obtain it. The well's position, close to the Kaaba yet below ground and out of the main circulation, reflects a long history of fitting a working well into a mosque that must also hold very large crowds. This record is a fact record about location and arrangement, and it gives distances as published approximations, since the mosque has been rebuilt and extended many times and any single measurement is tied to a particular layout.

demo.code:
import math
TITLE = 'Location Within the Grand Mosque'
FROM_CITY = 'Kaaba area (reference)'
FROM_LAT = 21.4225
FROM_LON = 39.8262
MECCA_LAT = 21.4225
MECCA_LON = 39.8262
R = 6371.0
p1 = math.radians(FROM_LAT); p2 = math.radians(MECCA_LAT)
dp = math.radians(MECCA_LAT - FROM_LAT); dl = math.radians(MECCA_LON - FROM_LON)
a = math.sin(dp/2)**2 + math.cos(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.sin(dl/2)**2
dist = 2*R*math.asin(math.sqrt(a))
y = math.sin(dl)*math.cos(p2); x = math.cos(p1)*math.sin(p2) - math.sin(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.cos(dl)
bearing = (math.degrees(math.atan2(y, x)) + 360) % 360
print('Place: ' + TITLE)
print('From: ' + FROM_CITY)
print('Great-circle distance to Mecca: %.1f km' % dist)
print('Initial bearing to Mecca: %.1f degrees' % bearing)
print('Method: haversine great-circle arithmetic on published coordinates; road distance differs.')

From: Kaaba area (reference)
Great-circle distance to Mecca: 0.0 km

title: Geology and Aquifer
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. The Zamzam aquifer is fed by rainfall on the hills surrounding Mecca, which drains into the Wadi Ibrahim valley floor and infiltrates through layers of sand and gravel that act as a natural preliminary filter before the water reaches deeper storage. The upper part of the well, about 13.5 metres according to published hydrogeological summaries, is excavated in the Wadi Ibrahim alluvium, unconsolidated sandy gravels and silts, and below that the well taps bedrock, so the water comes from two connected stores, the alluvium and the fractured rock. The Saudi Geological Survey has a Zamzam studies programme, reflecting the well's importance and the need to monitor a heavily used urban aquifer. This record is a fact record about published hydrogeology; where a thickness or depth is approximate, the record says so, because the well has been hand-expanded and reworked over a long period.

title: Well Depth and Structure
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. Published technical summaries describe the Zamzam Well as about 30 metres, or about 100 feet, deep, and 1.08 to 2.66 metres in diameter, with some published studies reporting 30.5 metres and others 35 metres, so this record gives the range rather than a single exact depth. The variation is understandable: the well was expanded by hand over many years, its upper section is in alluvium and its lower section in bedrock, and different surveys measured different points and different layouts. The well's structure is therefore best described as a hand-dug shaft, widened and deepened over time, with a modern basement well house and pumping arrangements at the top, rather than as a machine-drilled borehole of uniform diameter. This record is a fact record, and it states the range and the reason for the range, which is more honest than a false precision.

title: Water Extraction and Distribution
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. Zamzam water is moved by two electric pumps operating alternately, at a published pace of between 11 and 18.5 litres per second, about 5 kilometres southwards to the King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Zamzam Water Project in Kudai, which opened in September 2010 and cost a published 700 million Saudi riyals to construct. At Kudai the water is treated, using filters and ultraviolet light, stored, and distributed, and it is operated by the National Water Company of Saudi Arabia according to published references. From there it reaches dispensing points in the holy mosques and a bottling and public distribution centre outside the mosque for pilgrims who wish to carry it home. This record is a fact record about a documented engineering system; pumping rates are given as a published range because the pumps operate alternately and rates vary with demand and management.

title: Published Water-Quality Studies
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. Published water-quality studies of Zamzam water report its mineral composition and compare it with drinking-water guidelines, and this record reports what those studies found without adding any medical claim. A study published in 2011 examined 30 samples for metals, cations, anions, and other parameters, and reported average concentrations within World Health Organization permissible limits for all parameters except four, arsenic, nitrate, calcium, and potassium, whose averages were higher, at 27 micrograms per litre for arsenic and 120, 75, and 45 milligrams per litre for nitrate, calcium, and potassium respectively. Other published comparative studies report an alkaline pH of about 7.9 to 8.0 and total dissolved solids around 669 milligrams per litre, below the WHO maximum of 1,000 but above a stricter 500 milligram guideline used by some agencies. This record makes no claim that Zamzam water cures, treats, or prevents any condition, and it reports study results as dated published findings, not as this database's own testing.

The modern engineering of the Zamzam Well is organised around keeping a working well inside a mosque that must hold enormous crowds. The well opening sits in a basement room inaccessible to the public, where it can be seen behind glass panels, and two electric pumps operating alternately move the water south to Kudai for treatment, storage, and distribution. The basement arrangement, made in 1964 according to published references, freed the space above ground for pilgrims, and the Kudai plant, opened in 2010, separated treatment and bottling from the mosque itself. This record is a fact record about documented engineering arrangements, and it describes structures, not people: there are no diagrams of people in this pair, and no imagery of any prophet anywhere in this suite.

title: Monitoring
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. The Zamzam aquifer is monitored by the Saudi Geological Survey through its Zamzam studies programme, which reflects the need to watch water levels, quality, and pumping in a heavily used urban aquifer that also carries religious significance. Monitoring matters because the well's history includes periods when it became dry or was buried in sand, and because heavy pumping can lower water levels, a process described in published hydrogeological studies as overdrafting. Published monitoring therefore tracks the balance between recharge from rainfall on the surrounding hills and withdrawal by pumping, so that extraction can be managed rather than left to run unchecked. This record is a fact record about the existence and purpose of monitoring; it does not publish monitoring data of its own, and where such data is not in the public record consulted, the record says so.

title: Myths Corrected: Fact Versus Tradition

This record corrects common misunderstandings about Zamzam water by sorting each claim into fact or tradition, and it states plainly where a claim is neither. Fact: the well is about 30 metres deep, about 20 metres east of the Kaaba, and its water is pumped to Kudai for treatment and distribution. Tradition: the well's origin account involving Hagar and Ismail, and traditional sayings about the water's blessing, are tradition, and they are respected as tradition without being presented as measured history. Neither fact nor tradition: any claim that Zamzam water cures a specific disease is not established by the published studies reported here, and this pair makes no such claim; a study result in animals or in a small sample is not a cure. Where a claim is not in the public record, this record says it is not in the public record, rather than speculating.

title: Glossary: Zamzam Terms
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. This glossary defines the words used across the Zamzam pair, in plain language. An aquifer is a body of rock or sediment that stores and transmits groundwater. Alluvium is sand, gravel, and silt deposited by flowing water, and in Wadi Ibrahim it forms the upper store of the Zamzam aquifer. Bedrock is the solid rock beneath the alluvium, here the fractured basement rock that forms the lower store. Total dissolved solids means the combined dissolved mineral content of water, reported in milligrams per litre. Ultraviolet treatment means disinfecting water with ultraviolet light, used at Kudai alongside filtration. This record is a fact record of standard technical usage, and where a term also has a traditional use, the glossary says so and points to the tradition record for that meaning.

title: Engineering Timeline
description: This Signature edition record is an original Signature companion study for the same subject, written for this database and never presented as an authentic public record. It follows the public record's facts where they are stated, and it adds a Signature framing: how a reader can study, map, and compare the subject using only this database's own tools, demos, and cross-links. The engineering timeline of the Zamzam Well, as far as published references date it, runs from hand expansion over many years, through the rope-and-bucket era, to the modern pumping era. In 1964, according to published references, the well opening was placed in a basement room inaccessible to the public, freeing space above ground for pilgrims. In September 2010 the King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Zamzam Water Project opened in Kudai, at a published construction cost of 700 million Saudi riyals, and treatment, storage, and distribution moved there under the National Water Company of Saudi Arabia. Earlier dates in the well's history, including periods when it was dry or buried, are described in published histories in general terms rather than with exact years, and this record preserves that generality rather than inventing precise dates. This record is a fact record, dated only where published sources date an event.
